questions.stem: Several children admitted on the specialist pediatric gastroenterology ward developed loose stool. One 11-month child still in diapers had diarrhea and a fever >38°C; another 3-year child had diarrhea and vomiting; and one 5-year old child had vomiting only. All three had been on the unit for 3 weeks, with an underlying diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. Their symptoms began over a 48-hour period. Stool cultures for the 5-year-old were negative but were pending for the remaining two children. Blood results were unremarkable. Two staff members also reported vomiting over the preceding 24 hours.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Norovirus This fulfils Kaplan outbreak criteria for an outbreak as more than two patients related in time and space have developed similar symptoms. Norovirus is highly infectious and in this case has caused an outbreak. Although loose stool could be due to underlying inflammatory bowel disease in this population, vomiting is more indicative of norovirus, and even though the patients have been in hospital for 3 weeks, norovirus can often be introduced from the community, and the involvement of staff members here is highly suggestive. Accompanying fever is also commonly seen in norovirus infection, and there is no clear ingestion of a common food source to suggest Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus infection. Stool cultures should always be sent to exclude other enteric causes, and samples should also be tested for C. difficile as this can be commonly seen in patients with inflammatory bowel disease who receive multiple courses of antibiotics. Separate stool samples should be sent for norovirus as vomitus cannot be tested.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q17

questions.question: Concern of a healthcare setting outbreak.

parts.text: Define outbreak.
What are 4 early steps in an outbreak.
What are 2 agents that kill norovirus?

questions.model_answer:
a) A healthcare-associated outbreak is an increase in the number of cases of an infection/colonization (or a specific organism) above the number normally expected (baseline rate) in a defined population, over a defined time period, within a healthcare facility or unit, that is epidemiologically linked.
b) Initial/first steps of an outbreak investigation: (1) Confirm the existence of an outbreak (verify diagnosis and compare to baseline/expected rate). (2) Establish a case definition. (3) Actively search for and count cases (case finding, line listing). (4) Describe the outbreak by person, time, and place (descriptive epidemiology) to generate hypotheses, before implementing and evaluating control measures.
c) Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) solution and accelerated hydrogen peroxide are effective disinfectants against norovirus (routine quaternary-ammonium products are not reliably virucidal for norovirus).

questions.question: Norovirus infection

parts.text: 4 initial steps to outbreak investigation (yes, 4)
What two cleaning agents should you use.
What are 4 things you need to do to ensure people are properly protected when wearing N95 respirators?

questions.model_answer: a) Initial steps in outbreak investigation (4): (1) verify the diagnosis/confirm an outbreak exists (2) establish a case definition and identify cases (3) implement immediate control measures (isolation/cohorting) (4) notify public health and relevant stakeholders. b) Cleaning agents for norovirus: sodium hypochlorite (bleach) solution and a detergent/EPA-registered virucidal disinfectant effective against norovirus (non-enveloped virus, resistant to alcohol alone). c) Ensuring proper N95 protection (4): (1) fit-testing specific to the model used (2) seal check (user fit-check) each time it is donned (3) no facial hair interfering with the seal (4) proper storage/limited reuse per protocol and discard if damaged or moist.

questions.question: An 84 year-old resident of a long-term care facility develops severe diarrhea. Stool PCR is positive for Norovirus.

parts.text: What family does this virus belong to?
What type of genetic material does this virus have?
Is the genetic material single-stranded or double-stranded?
List TWO infection prevention strategies that should be implemented.

questions.model_answer:
a) Family: Caliciviridae.
b) Genetic material: RNA.
c) Single-stranded (positive-sense).
d) Infection prevention: (1) contact precautions (gown/gloves) with cohorting of ill patients and dedicated equipment, (2) hand hygiene with soap and water (alcohol-based sanitizer is less effective against norovirus) plus environmental cleaning/disinfection with a sporicidal/norovirus-effective (e.g., bleach-based) disinfectant; restrict ill staff/visitors and close affected units to new admissions during outbreaks.
questions.beyond_mandell: General virology/IPAC knowledge (CDC/PHAC norovirus outbreak management guidance); chapter not available in this question bank's page set.

questions.question: You see a patient with severe sepsis. He recently traveled to Florida where he consumed many raw oysters.

parts.text: What is the most likely bacteria causing his infection?
List THREE clinical syndromes associated with this bacteria.
List THREE risk factors for severe sepsis with this bacteria.
List TWO common viral infections that are associated with eating raw oysters.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely bacteria: Vibrio vulnificus.
b) 3 clinical syndromes: (1) primary septicemia (often fulminant bacteremia), (2) wound infection/necrotizing skin and soft tissue infection (from seawater/shellfish exposure), (3) gastroenteritis.
c) 3 risk factors for severe sepsis: (1) chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, (2) iron overload states (e.g., hemochromatosis), (3) immunocompromising conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, chronic renal disease, or immunosuppressive therapy).
d) 2 viral infections associated with raw oyster consumption: norovirus and hepatitis A virus.

questions.question: There is a norovirus outbreak (?at a nursing home).

parts.text: What is the incubation period for norovirus?
For a previously healthy person, what are the symptoms of norovirus and how long do they last?
What is the diagnostic test?
What feature about norovirus make it difficult to contain an outbreak?

questions.model_answer:
a) Incubation period: 12–48 hours (typically ~24-48h).
b) Symptoms in a previously healthy person: acute-onset nausea, vomiting, watery non-bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, +/- low-grade fever and myalgia; usually self-limited, lasting 24–72 hours (1–3 days).
c) Diagnostic test: stool PCR (RT-PCR) for norovirus RNA (most sensitive; antigen EIA is less sensitive).
d) Feature limiting outbreak control: very low infectious dose (as few as 10-100 viral particles), prolonged environmental persistence/resistance to routine disinfectants and alcohol-based sanitizers, multiple transmission routes (fecal-oral, vomitus aerosolization, fomites, contaminated food/water), prolonged viral shedding after symptom resolution, and high genetic/antigenic diversity limiting durable immunity.
questions.beyond_mandell: General ID/virology knowledge (CDC norovirus guidance); chapter not available in this question bank's page set.

parts.text: Incubation period
Symptoms and duration of symptomatic illness
Despite fomites and fecal-oral transmission why is it so challenging to prevent spread

cohort_answer.text:
Incubation period: Approximately 24-48 hours, although ranges from 18 to 72 hours have been observed.
Symptoms and duration: Nausea, vomiting (non-bloody, non-bilious), watery diarrhea (non-bloody) with abdominal pain; generalized myalgias, malaise, headache prominent; fever in approximately half of cases. Symptoms typically last 48-72 hours with rapid recovery.
Why challenging to prevent spread: High infectivity with low infectious dose (<100 viral particles required); asymptomatic shedding (mean duration of viral shedding 4 weeks after onset of illness); environmental stability (resists freezing, heating to 60°C, disinfection with chlorine/alcohol).

parts.text: A) Incubation period
B. Classic clinical symptoms in immunocompetent host, and duration
C. Most sensitive test for detection of infection
D. Other than fomites / fecal-oral, what accounts for the high rate of secondary infection

cohort_answer.text:
A: Generally 24-48 hours, but range is 18-72 hours.

B: Often nausea/vomiting prominent, along with diarrhea; abdominal cramps and low grade fever may be present. Duration usually 12-60 hours. Viral shedding maximal for first 24-48 hours after illness.

C: rt-PCR for virus in stool.

D: Resistance to inactivation with chlorine, alcohol and heat/cooling. Environmental stability. Small inoculum required for transmission (<100 particles). Role of pre-symptomatic food handlers in spreading disease. Potential role of airborne droplet transmission via vomit.

parts.text: A. What type of virus and the family?
B. Mechanism of transmission:
C. Two things shown to reduce transmission:
D. Diagnosis mechanisms and their limitations?

cohort_answer.text:
A: Family Caliciviridae, genera Norovirus and Sapovirus. ss, positive sense, non-enveloped RNA virus; each has multiple genogroups and genotypes

B: Fecal-oral, with fomites and contaminated food/water by food handlers contributing to infectivity and high secondary attack rate. Implicated foods include sandwiches and salads, particularly salad greens.

C: Excluding ill employees from work until 48-72 hours after symptom resolution; identify and eliminate common sources; use hand washing and barrier methods (not killed by alcohol based hand disinfection); decontaminate fomites with concentrated bleach or other approved solution; use contact precautions in hospital.

D: rt-PCR for virus in stool most sensitive. ELISA has reduced sensitivity. Electron microscopy no longer used.

parts.text: What family of viruses does it belong to?
What is the nucleic acid composition?
Is it single or double stranded?
Name 2 infection prevention recommendations for limiting spread

cohort_answer.text: Family: Caliciviridae. Nucleic acid: Small nonenveloped ribonucleic acid (RNA). Strand: Single stranded. Prevention: Contact precautions (add droplet if vomiting); Hand hygiene (soap and water, not killed by alcohol); Environmental cleaning (bleach); Exclude HCW who have symptoms until 48-72h after symptom resolution; individual with norovirus should not prepare food for others until at least 2 days after resolution of symptoms
